newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwandan refugees confound U.N. refugee agency.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees confound U.N. refugee agency.

text.p: Rwandan refugees are showing a remarkable ability to confound planners of the U.N. refugee agency which cared for and fed them at a cost of $1 million per day for two years.

The mood of officials of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) turned from despair to ecstasy on Friday as they watched tens of thousands of refugees stop in their tracks when confronted by roadblocks set up by Tanzanian troops.
They then turned round and headed back to their camps.
But aid workers said UNHCR officials were restricted from moving by Tanzanian authorities, apparently so they could not witness refugees being barred from the camps by stick-wielding troops.

Seeing no alternative, some crossed back into Rwanda while thousands of others tried to run past the Tanzanian cordon and back into Benaco camp, which more than 100,000 refugees abandoned on Thursday.

"Refugees move or don't move for one reason and one reason only: fear. That's why they're refugees," said a U.N. official who has long watched UNHCR's carefully laid plans effectively trampled underfoot by the Rwandan refugees of Central Africa.
"UNHCR cannot make them fear, except slightly in this case by hinting that Tanzania may expel them, so it cannot alone make them move and cannot determine which direction they move in," he added.
"Therefore they frequently move in the opposite direction to what UNHCR wants, or they move at the wrong time in the right direction. But they almost always catch UNHCR by surprise," he said.

The UNHCR was surprised last month when an estimated 500,000 Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire flooded back into Rwanda after fighting between Zairean rebels and troops forced them out of their camps.
"We never expected them to come back in mass," said a UNHCR spokesman after journalists told him UNHCR should have expected them to return in the same sized groups as they left Rwanda in 1994.
The agency's credibility and competence were challenged at the highest level last month when its figures for the number of Rwandan refugees in Zaire were presented as grossly exaggerated.
Some of the Western governments under pressure to help the refugees avoided doing so partly by denying that the UNHCR's 1.1 million census was even vaguely accurate.
U.S. military planners, for instance, said they could account for only 700,000 refugees.
Why it took donors who funded the agency's refugee operations for two years so long to decide the numbers were wrong is a mystery.
The UNHCR was surprised last Sunday when the Rwandan refugees in Tanzania started leaving their camps and heading away from the Rwandan border instead of towards it as the agency wanted.

UNHCR officials saw refugees packing their belongings and assumed they were about to return home voluntarily in a success for the UNHCR-Tanzanian government plan for all 540,000 Rwandan refugees in northwest Tanzania to go back by December 31.
UNHCR organised for each of the refugees to receive a two-week ration of food and for aid agencies to pay off Rwandans who had worked for them in an attempt to coax them to go home.
Instead they left the camps and headed in the opposite direction, saying they would walk to Kenya or Malawi rather than fall victim to what they believed would be a plan to expel them.
"I don't care, I just don't care. I'm going home," said an exasperated UNHCR official on hearing that agency colleagues were disputing his estimate of the size of the refugee exodus.

UNHCR officials said the refugees were the victims of a carefully orchestrated plan of intimidation by Hutu hardliners in the camps who fear reprisals or punishment in Rwanda for their role in the genocide of up to one million people in 1994.

"They (intimidators) have fooled us incredibly," said Anne Willem Bijleveld, who had been in charge of the plan to entice the refugees home, taking advantage of what it thought would be the momentum generated by the mass return from Zaire last month.
